dz.headline: Attaf denies Algeria ordered a boycott of French goods
dz.dek: The foreign minister said French suppliers lost ground on price and competition, and urged Paris to use the EU-Algeria Association Council to discuss the dispute.
paragraphs: Algerian Foreign Minister Ahmed Attaf denied on Thursday in Algiers that the government had ordered French products excluded from its market. France has decided to take the issue to the European Commission, according to media reports cited by the account.

Attaf said French operators’ declining market share reflected economic factors, not political instructions. He said Algeria was willing to discuss the dispute at the EU-Algeria Association Council, which he described as the institutional forum for disagreements between the parties to their agreement.

Attaf said Algeria changed its wheat supplier rules in 2021, opening procurement to new operators, including Romania, because of price and competition. He also said Algeria now buys milk powder from the Netherlands and Poland on terms he described as more acceptable than France’s. He said data through October 2026 contradicted French allegations.

dz.headline: Algeria bars construction and fuel freight during local elections
dz.dek: The Gendarmerie says the restriction runs until 05:00 on 29 November, while food deliveries remain exempt.
paragraphs: Algeria’s National Gendarmerie has barred trucks carrying construction materials or fuel, and freight trains, from operating from midnight on 27 November until 05:00 on 29 November, during local elections scheduled for 28 November.

The restriction covers cargo such as gravel, sand and wood, but not vehicles supplying food, including milk, flour, meat, fruit and vegetables, the Gendarmerie said in a statement on its Tariki Facebook page. The locally competent wali, or governor, can grant exceptional permits for fuel tanker movements.
The Interior Ministry’s order of 16 November provides for restrictions on freight vehicles during the 27–29 November period, the Gendarmerie said.

dz.headline: Algeria issues orange rain alerts for 22 wilayas
dz.dek: The meteorological office forecasts 20 to 40 mm in some areas, after farmers raised concern over a lack of rain during ploughing.
paragraphs: Algeria’s National Office of Meteorology issued orange rain alerts for 22 wilayas on Friday 27 November, forecasting up to 40 mm in some regions. The first alert covered 11 wilayas, where 20 to 30 mm was expected from 03 du matin to 15h00.

A second alert covered Tizi Ouzou, Béjaïa, Jijel, Skikda, Annaba and El Tarf, with 20 to 40 mm forecast between 06h00 and 23h00. Biskra, Batna, Khenchela, Tébessa and El Oued were under alert from 13h00 to 22h00, with 20 to 30 mm expected.
The office issued the warnings after a prolonged hot summer and concern among farmers over a shortage of rain during the ploughing period. The report also said forest fires had occurred in November.

dz.headline: Algerian army seizes more than a million pregabalin tablets in In Salah
dz.dek: The army said two traffickers were killed on Wednesday, 25 November, after refusing orders to stop while trying to bring the tablets into Algeria.
paragraphs: An Algerian army detachment killed two drug traffickers in In Salah, in the country’s far south, on Wednesday, 25 November, and seized more than a million pregabalin tablets, the Defence Ministry said. The men were trying to bring the pills into Algeria, the ministry said.

The ministry said the traffickers tried to flee and refused to obey orders. Soldiers also seized two metal detectors, two off-road vehicles, two satellite phones and two transmission devices during the operation.
The ministry said army units across Algeria were ready to confront criminal networks and stop attempts to bring drugs into the country. Its statement did not give a date for further action.

ao.headline: Carrinho Agri invests millions in farm operations platform
ao.dek: The Angola-built system is designed to track production and logistics and connect farmers, suppliers, banks and insurers.
paragraphs: Carrinho Agri is investing several million dollars in a technology platform to manage agricultural operations in Angola, the company’s chief executive, David Maciel, said in Luanda on Thursday. The investment amount was not disclosed.

The system, called the Carrinho Integrated Production System, is designed to identify producers, map their growing areas and track technical support needs, inputs and crop collection. The company says it will also connect farmers with suppliers, logistics operators, banks and insurers.

The spending includes computer equipment and worker training, Maciel said. Carrinho Agri is also developing the platform’s climate information tools and considering a link with Brazil’s agricultural research company, Embrapa. The system is intended to incorporate new technologies, including artificial intelligence.

ao.headline: Angola's stock exchange records 6.95 billion kwanzas in trades
ao.dek: The 25 November session included 308 deals in 32 securities, while five of the seven listed companies closed higher.
paragraphs: Angola's Debt and Securities Exchange (BODIVA), the country's capital markets body, recorded 6.95 billion kwanzas in trading on Wednesday, 25 November. The session saw 308 deals involving 32 securities: seven shares and 25 debt instruments.

Five of the seven listed companies ended higher. Unitel led gains, rising 1.81% to 27,999 kwanzas, followed by Standard Bank Angola, up 1.75% to 58,000 kwanzas, and the power company ENSA, up 1.73% to 23,400 kwanzas. BODIVA shares fell 2.91% to 100,000 kwanzas, while Banco Angolano de Investimentos lost 1.67% to close at 93,900 kwanzas.
Treasury bonds accounted for the largest reported trades: OJ15I31A bonds drew approximately 3.1 billion kwanzas, and OH15N28D bonds 1.3 billion kwanzas.

ao.headline: Tranquilidade Seguros Angola names new chair under FAST29 plan
ao.dek: José Octávio Serra Van-Dúnem takes the board role as former chair Artur Fonseca Duarte moves to lead the insurer’s executive committee.
paragraphs: Tranquilidade Seguros Angola appointed José Octávio Serra Van-Dúnem as board chair as it reorganised its governance and launched FAST29, a strategy running to 2029. Artur Fonseca Duarte, the former chair, will lead the executive committee, overseeing operations and implementation of the insurer’s strategy.

The insurer said the changes are intended to strengthen governance, consolidate its position in Angola’s market and improve competitiveness.

ao.headline: Brazil's National Library puts 108 Angolan archival volumes online
ao.dek: The free digital copies include official correspondence and records on populations, trade and political relations, while the originals stay in Angola.
paragraphs: Brazil's National Library has made 108 digitised volumes from Angola's National Archive available online for free, opening records on the countries' historical ties to researchers. The release took place in Rio de Janeiro during the "Travessias" meeting on Angolan manuscripts and Brazil's Resgate project.

The volumes contain official correspondence, royal letters, permits and administrative reports, with material on populations, territories, commerce and political relations. Heliodoro Abambres, deputy director-general for technical and scientific affairs at Angola's National Archive, said the records could support research into the transatlantic slave trade, including how Africans were classified and taxed as merchandise.

The originals remain in Angola; only digital reproductions were released. The 108 volumes represent less than 1% of the archive's preserved documentary collection, Abambres said. The release follows a memorandum signed by the two institutions in March 2026.

bj.headline: Benin proposes CFA174,826 billion for health in 2027
bj.dek: Health Minister Benjamin Ignace Bodounrin Hounkpatin told lawmakers the funds would support urgent care, new hospitals and existing facilities.
paragraphs: Benin’s health minister, Benjamin Ignace Bodounrin Hounkpatin, presented a proposed CFA174,826 billion allocation for 2027 to lawmakers in Porto-Novo on Wednesday, 25 November. The plan covers emergency care for patients in immediate danger, reducing maternal and newborn deaths, building new zone hospitals, and upgrading and equipping existing facilities.

The ministry also plans to recruit more than 500 contract agents, train more than 200 specialist doctors and train 60 hospital interns. The proposed health allocation was presented as lawmakers considered the 2027 finance bill, which has been sent to the National Assembly.

The finance bill totals 4 CFA757 billion. Other proposed ministry allocations include CFA11,59 billion for digital affairs, down about 30%, and CFA20,778 billion for foreign affairs, up 13,79% from 2026.

bj.headline: Japan funds Benin malaria pilot with two spray drones
bj.dek: The $2.3 million programme also supplies 12 backpack sprayers for mosquito-control work in 10 districts through February 2027.
paragraphs: Japan-funded partners handed Benin's Health Ministry two TSUBASA CT110 spraying drones, 12 Maruyama MD300 backpack sprayers and other equipment in Cotonou on Thursday, 26 November. The equipment is for a malaria-prevention pilot costing $2.3 million, or more than CFA1.33 billion.

The programme combines digital tools, treatment of mosquito breeding sites and community involvement, with drones intended for spraying in targeted areas and backpack units for manual work. UNICEF's Benin representative, Ousmane Niang, said early results in the north showed a reduction in larval density in targeted areas. Health Minister Benjamin Hounkpatin said his department would oversee proper use of the equipment.

Launched on 30 June, the pilot covers 10 districts and is scheduled to run for 12 months, from March 2026 to February 2027. Its northern locations are Tchaourou, Djougou and Copargo; seven others are in the south.

bj.headline: Wadagni secures initial agreement for eight-country UEMOA summit in 2027
bj.dek: The Beninese president consulted leaders from Burkina Faso, Mali and Niger after months of deadlock over holding a top-level meeting.
paragraphs: Benin’s President Romuald Wadagni has secured an agreement in principle to bring the leaders of the eight-member West African Economic and Monetary Union (UEMOA) together in early 2027, according to reporting by Africa Intelligence cited by La Nouvelle Tribune. The proposed summit follows several months of deadlock over arranging a leaders’ meeting.

Preparations included discreet consultations with the military authorities in Burkina Faso, Mali and Niger. The three countries remain in UEMOA despite leaving the Economic Community of West African States. The agenda is expected to include reforming the union’s statutes, renewing mandates in its bodies and discussing the common currency and monetary integration.
The reported agreement does not settle all arrangements for the meeting. Benin Web TV also reported that institutional reform is among the subjects under consideration.

bj.headline: Benin, Senegal and Djibouti set plans for out-of-school youth training
bj.dek: A Cotonou meeting reviewed the three-country training scheme and outlined national rollout plans, trainer preparation and field monitoring.
paragraphs: Benin, Senegal and Djibouti are preparing national plans to train professionals who support young people outside school, after a meeting in Cotonou on Wednesday, 25 November. The meeting was organised by the Conference of Education Ministers of French-speaking Countries (CONFEMEN), a body that groups the ministers responsible for education in francophone states.

Benin's secondary education minister, Adéyèmi Clément Kouchadé, opened the talks and said the next steps include national rollout plans, training of relays and supervisors, new training sessions and monitoring of skills in the field. Participants reviewed national workshops and a knowledge-sharing meeting in Dakar before drawing up an action plan for each country.

The meeting was due to end on 26 November and to prepare a regional framework for 2026-2028 to anchor the scheme in the three countries. CONFEMEN secretary-general Abdel Rahamane Baba-Moussa said alternative education pathways have become essential for young people facing difficulties.

bj.headline: Benin plans a learning city in each of its six development hubs
bj.dek: Decentralisation Minister Janvier Yahouédéhou presented the plan in Cotonou and cited Porto-Novo, admitted to UNESCO's learning-cities network in 2025, as the model.
paragraphs: Benin's government wants at least one learning city in each of the country's six territorial development hubs, Decentralisation and Local Governance Minister Janvier Yahouédéhou said on Thursday, 26 November, at the Palais des Congrès in Cotonou. He set out the ambition before municipal officials from several African countries.

The principle is to widen access to training beyond the school system. Municipalities can use libraries, community centres, vocational training colleges and workplaces so that residents keep learning at any age. The minister linked infrastructure and economic activity to the skills of residents.

Porto-Novo, the administrative capital, joined UNESCO's global network of learning cities in 2025. Its programmes include literacy, business management and microcredit for women entrepreneurs, and the city's École d'entrepreneuriat offers young people training in commerce and management. The African conference, held with UNESCO's Institute for Lifelong Learning on 26 and 27 November, will present certificates to newly admitted cities.

bw.headline: Botswana businesses face 72-hour data breach reporting window
bw.dek: Under the Data Protection Act, controllers must alert the commission without undue delay, and high-risk breaches also require notice to affected people.
paragraphs: Under Botswana’s Data Protection Act, 2024, the organisations that control personal data must alert the Information and Data Protection Commission without undue delay, and within 72 hours of awareness where that is feasible. Where a breach is likely to pose a high risk to people’s rights and freedoms, those people must be told too, subject to the Act’s exceptions.

Air Botswana’s suspected ransomware incident, identified on November 3, 2026, has put the rules in focus. The airline said affected internal systems held employee and internal information, while passenger booking, aircraft and flight operations were unaffected. It said it had activated its response procedures and engaged the relevant authorities.

The Act took effect on January 14, 2025. Section 63 places the duty to notify the commission on the controller, the organisation that decides why and how personal data is used, not on a service provider that processes data for it.

Where a breach is likely to pose a high risk to people’s rights and freedoms, those people must be told too, subject to the Act’s exceptions.

Air Botswana’s suspected ransomware incident, identified on November 3, 2026, has put the rules in focus. The airline said affected internal systems held employee and internal information, while passenger booking, aircraft and flight operations were unaffected. It said it had activated its response procedures and engaged the relevant authorities.

The Act took effect on January 14, 2025. Section 63 places the duty to notify the commission on the controller, the organisation that decides why and how personal data is used, not on a service provider that processes data for it.

bw.headline: Botswana law gives consumers a stop to AI-driven direct marketing
bw.dek: The Data Protection Act lets people object at any time to using their personal data for direct marketing, including related profiling.
paragraphs: Botswana’s Data Protection Act, 2024, regulates how organisations process personal data, including information used to personalise advertising with artificial intelligence (AI). The law took effect on 14 January 2025.

Under section 48(3), individuals can object at any time to processing their data for direct marketing and related profiling. Once someone objects, section 48(4) requires that the data no longer be processed for those purposes. Organisations must clearly and separately explain the right at their first communication, including in WhatsApp broadcasts, texts, calls, email newsletters and social media advertising.

The rules also apply to businesses that collect phone numbers through promotions, keep mailing lists or use AI to analyse purchases. Companies using outside AI tools are responsible for checking how providers handle, retain and protect customer information, including whether it crosses borders.

bf.headline: Burkina Faso reviews study of maternal and child mortality declines
bf.dek: Research partners presented findings in Ouagadougou after maternal mortality fell 47% and deaths of children under five fell 78% from 1998 to 2021.
paragraphs: Burkina Faso’s health ministry and research partners reviewed final findings on what contributed to falling maternal and child mortality at a two-day workshop in Ouagadougou on Nov. 24 and 25. The study, begun in 2024, was conducted with Northwestern University and the Institute for Disease Modeling.

The 2021 Demographic and Health Survey recorded a 47% reduction in maternal mortality and a 78% decline in deaths of children under five between 1998 and 2021, ministry technical adviser Estelle-Edith Dembélé/Dabiré said. She said the progress came amid security and humanitarian challenges, as well as limits on access to and availability of health services.

Participants discussed recommendations intended to strengthen the health system. The ministry said the research sought to identify which system factors and interventions contributed to the declines and help guide health policy.

bf.headline: AUXFIN Burkina Faso seeks infrastructure pledges for rural communities
bf.dek: The social enterprise, AUXFIN Burkina Faso, brought partners together in Ouagadougou to present community needs and seek commitments to meet them.
paragraphs: AUXFIN Burkina Faso, a social enterprise, brought partners and institutions together in Ouagadougou on Thursday 26 November 2026 to present rural communities' infrastructure needs and seek commitments to address them. The company says it supports nearly 200 000 direct beneficiaries in more than 4 350 community groups of about 50 households each, known as G50 groups.

Its director general, Serge Diasso, said the groups include more than 700 000 indirect beneficiaries. The company has distributed more than 4 300 digital tablets across communities in 13 of the country's 17 regions. The tablets carry applications offering training in farming practices, financial education and food processing, as well as access to farm inputs, microcredit, formal savings and marketing opportunities.

The company said its e-Coachs applications turn training material into videos, translate it into local languages and share it with beneficiaries, helping offset a shortage of agricultural extension agents in rural areas.

bf.headline: Burkinabè researcher wins US patent and urges 1 000 annual applications
bf.dek: Moïse Convolbo’s predictive artificial-intelligence system was developed in Japan at Rakuten after nearly six years and five provisional refusals.
paragraphs: Burkinabè researcher Dr Moïse Convolbo received a US patent on 24 November 2026 for an artificial-intelligence system that predicts users’ decisions on digital services. Developed in Japan within the Rakuten group, it is designed to identify a visitor’s behaviour while they are still using a service, without removing their freedom to choose.

Convolbo told Lefaso.net that the system learned from many visitors’ online journeys, including pages viewed, click order and returns to earlier pages, alongside how each visit ended. He said the invention began with online shoppers who browse and compare products but leave without completing a purchase; conventional tools analyse such departures only afterward.

The patent followed nearly six years of proceedings and five provisional refusals, according to the report. Convolbo called for Burkina Faso to set a target of 1 000 patent applications a year and for closer ties between African research and markets.

bf.headline: Burkina Faso hosts China-focused forum on cultural and human exchange
bf.dek: The 26-27 November gathering at the University of Burkina brings together students, Chinese diplomats, experts and businesspeople, alongside participants from Gabon, Cameroon.
paragraphs: Burkina Faso’s Club of Young People for the Promotion of Sino-Burkinabè Cooperation opened its seventh international forum on Thursday, 26 November, at the University of Burkina in Ouagadougou. The two-day event focuses on cultural and human exchange between China and Burkina Faso.

The organisers say students, staff from China’s embassy, experts and businesspeople are taking part in discussions on human, commercial and cultural ties. Abdoul Razahagou Dénié, the club’s national coordinator, said participants would consider China’s revolution as a source of ideas for Burkina Faso’s development. Delegations from Gabon, Cameroon and Senegal are also attending.

Jean-Noël Bonkoungou, representing the culture minister, urged Burkinabè students who study in China to return and apply their expertise at home. China’s ambassador, Zhao Deyong, said the embassy had conducted human and cultural activities with Burkinabè government bodies and associations during 2026.

bi.headline: Cholera infects 12 Saint-Marc pupils as Bujumbura water shortage persists
bi.dek: Seven pupils were taken to hospital Wednesday and five more Thursday; the boarding school has reportedly lacked drinking water for nearly two weeks.
paragraphs: At least 12 pupils at Lycée Saint-Marc, a boarding school in Bujumbura, have contracted cholera since Wednesday, SOS Médias Burundi reported. Seven were taken to Prince Régent Charles Hospital on Wednesday and five more on Thursday.

Pupils link the cases to a shortage of drinking water that they say has lasted about two weeks, and called for authorities to restore supply. Parents say the school’s management has refused to let pupils return to their families; pupils also say their parents were not informed. The school confirmed cholera cases but declined to give more details.
Eight people were reportedly affected in Bwiza, while cases were also reported in Cibitoke. Administrative officials confirmed those reports without providing further details.

bi.headline: Burundi transfers four Mpimba figures to three prisons
bi.dek: The former director and two officials are accused of granting businessperson Aloys Ntakarutimana privileges during his detention at Mpimba.
paragraphs: Burundi’s intelligence service transferred four people from its Bujumbura cells to prisons around the country on Tuesday, 24 November. The group includes Jimmy Ndayishimiye, the former director of Mpimba prison, social affairs officer Spès Caritas Shurweryimana, prison police official Fortuné Habonimana and businessperson Aloys Ntakarutimana, known as Wakenya.

SOS Médias Burundi reported that Ndayishimiye was taken to Gitega prison, while Shurweryimana and Habonimana went to Muramvya central prison. Ntakarutimana was returned to Mpimba. The three prison officials are suspected of giving him privileges, including permission to leave for medical care; no official statement has set out the reasons for the transfers or formal charges.

Ntakarutimana is accused of doing business in an area of eastern Democratic Republic of Congo controlled by the M23. Burundi’s forces are fighting the group alongside Congo’s army. No judicial next step has been announced.

bi.headline: Burundi trafficking networks use five routes to send children to Tanzania
bi.dek: An advocacy group says the routes cross several provinces and urges the government to strengthen enforcement and revise the 2014 trafficking law.
paragraphs: Trafficking networks use at least five clandestine routes across Burundi to send children to neighbouring Tanzania, according to the ONLCT, a Burundian anti-trafficking organisation. The routes cross several provinces and remain operational, the group said.

Prime Mbarubukeye, the organisation’s legal representative, said authorities intercepted 253 Burundian children on trafficking routes in Rutana in 2025. Of those children, 118 had left their families during school holidays, particularly in July and August, heading for Tanzania. The group identified five routes, including crossings toward Kigoma and one from Mwaro to Mabanda, where children are reportedly taken onward by motorbike.

The organisation is asking the government to amend the 2014 law on preventing and punishing human trafficking and protecting victims. It says the law should cover newer forms of child exploitation through digital platforms and social networks.

cm.headline: Cameroon lifts domestic share of public investment funding to 62.6%
cm.dek: Finance Minister Louis Paul Motaze said domestic funding rose by CFA261 billion in 2025, while external funding fell by CFA13.9 billion.
paragraphs: Cameroon financed 62.6% of its Public Investment Budget from domestic resources in 2025, Finance Minister Louis Paul Motaze told the National Assembly’s Finance and Budget Committee on November 25. The share was 55.9% in 2024 and 46.8% in 2023, according to the Ministry of Economy, Planning and Regional Development.

Motaze said domestic funding allocated to public investment rose by CFA261 billion from 2024, while external funding declined by CFA13.9 billion. Domestic resources overtook external financing in 2024, when they accounted for more than half of the investment budget for the first time in five years, the ministry said.

The ministry linked the shift partly to a new government budget classification system and reforms begun in 2022 to change how externally financed projects are budgeted. Domestic funding also had higher spending execution rates, according to the government’s budget execution report.

cm.headline: Cameroon seeks $1.53 billion from investors and donors for farm overhaul
cm.dek: Most of the $1.87 billion needed for the AgriConnect programme is expected to come from private investors and development partners rather than the state.
paragraphs: Cameroon expects private investors and international development partners to provide $1.53 billion of the $1.87 billion needed for its AgriConnect agricultural transformation programme from 2026 to 2030. The national compact was launched in Yaoundé on October 21, 2026, according to a programme document published by the World Bank Group.

The government expects to contribute $336 million, about 18% of the total. The document does not say how the $1.53 billion will be split between investors and development partners, or how much has already been secured.

Cameroon plans to attract funding through financial risk-sharing and public-private partnerships, with at least 10 such partnerships targeted. A credit guarantee mechanism is meant to generate CFA10 billion in agricultural lending, but details of eligible borrowers, participating lenders and risk coverage have not been disclosed.

cm.headline: Cameroon opens study for first national electricity tariff policy
cm.dek: Consultations began in Yaoundé on November 25 to examine pricing principles, social tariffs, targeted subsidies and equalization.
paragraphs: Cameroon’s Ministry of Water and Energy began work on the country’s first national electricity tariff policy, opening consultations in Yaoundé on November 25, 2026. The consultations will review the scope of a study to guide the proposed framework, which is intended to set clearer rules for electricity prices.

A ministry representative speaking for the water and energy minister said the lack of a national policy had contributed to inconsistent contractual practices and unpredictable pricing decisions. The study will assess social tariffs for eligible households, subsidies for specific consumer groups and equalization to address different prices paid by comparable consumers across geographic areas.
The framework is intended to balance affordability for consumers with the power sector’s financial needs. No new rates, subsidy amounts or eligibility criteria have been announced.

cm.headline: Cameroon opens 82.252-kilometre road serving 22 villages
cm.dek: The Awae-Esse-Soa route links three communes and connects to national roads 1, 4 and 10, with access toward the Central African Republic.
paragraphs: Cameroon’s public works minister, Emmanuel Nganou Djoumessi, officially opened the 82.252-kilometre Awae-Esse-Soa road on Thursday, linking three communes in the Mefou and Afamba department. The road serves 22 villages and joins national roads 1, 4 and 10.

The Ministry of Public Works said the new route will help move macabo, cassava and plantain to national and regional markets faster. The project, funded with CFA76.61 billion from the public investment budget, was built by China First Highway Engineering Company Cameroon and generated 943 jobs, including 919 for Cameroonians.

The works also included a two-by-two-lane urban crossing in Esse, 5,000 square metres of parking in Soa and 25 hand-pumped wells along the route. Connections through the national roads extend toward the Central African Republic.

cm.headline: MPEC seeks to unseat ruling party in Dja and Lobo’s five seats
cm.dek: Professor Jean-Calvin Aba’a Oyono leads a six-person slate challenging the ruling party’s hold on the department’s National Assembly seats.
paragraphs: Professor Jean-Calvin Aba’a Oyono has filed to contest Cameroon’s 2027 legislative elections in Dja and Lobo, leading a Mouvement populaire pour l’émergence du Cameroun (MPEC) slate seeking all five National Assembly seats held by the ruling Rassemblement démocratique du peuple camerounais (RDPC). The department is in the South region.

The list includes MPEC national president Martine Danielle Befolo Essono, Thomas Dydime Tomo Ze, Edjimbi Epse Nkoumou Nkoumsu and Jean Cyrille Abondo Ngono, as well as their respective substitutes. The Electoral Council must decide whether to accept the slate before the candidates can compete.

Aba’a Oyono was detained for a month after protests over the results of the 12 October 2025 presidential election, the report says. He later filed appeals against external intelligence services and Defence personnel.

cf.headline: Central African Republic launches three price-monitoring commissions
cf.dek: Set up by the prime minister on 10 November, the committee began work in Bangui on 25 November to address the high cost of living.
paragraphs: The Central African Republic’s joint committee on social measures and prices began work in Bangui on 25 November, with three commissions assigned to monitor prices and supplies across the country. The prime minister created the committee on 10 November to address the high cost of living.

Committee president Arnaud Djoubaye Abazène said the commissions will check prices for essential goods, urban and intercity transport fares, and the supply of petroleum products nationwide. The committee’s remit covers both costs paid by households and the availability of fuel.
The committee officially launched its work at a ceremony in Bangui, Radio Ndeke Luka reported. Its stated duties include monitoring the three areas; no further measures or deadlines were reported.

cf.headline: Audit rates Bangui and Bouboui abattoirs 39% compliant
cf.dek: A government-commissioned review found hygiene and safety failures and says the operator did not pay the state its contractual share of revenue.
paragraphs: A government-commissioned audit found the state-run abattoir company, the Société d'État de Gestion des Abattoirs, was only 39% compliant at its Bangui and Bouboui sites, based on an assessment covering 2023 to September 2025. The review followed inspections at both sites and a survey of 87 butchers.

The interministerial committee reported poor hygiene, breaches of health and environmental standards, weak services and workplace risks. It also said Dibro Service, the company contracted to run the abattoirs, had not paid the state the 25% of operating revenue required by its contract. Government controller Roméo Gribingui said the conditions threatened public health, including that of beef consumers, and that waste from slaughter was discharged into the Oubangui River.

Dibro Service chief executive Ibrahim Dibro disputed the audit, calling it partial and saying it omitted unfulfilled state commitments under the contract. The government signed the 20-year operating contract with the company in October 2022.

cf.headline: African Development Bank warns of hidden PPP costs to Central African finances
cf.dek: The bank says infrastructure deals carry real future payment commitments whose cost remains largely outside public accounts.
paragraphs: The African Development Bank has warned that public-private partnership contracts used to finance major infrastructure projects in the Central African Republic carry future costs that threaten state finances. The commitments are real, the bank says, but much of their cost is not visible in public accounts.

The bank described a potential debt burden that is not recorded in those accounts but will have to be paid in the future. Its warning concerns the contracts signed to fund large infrastructure projects; the report gives no cost estimate or payment schedule.
The warning focuses on the future obligations created by those agreements and their effect on the state’s finances.

cf.headline: MSF adds 52-bed paediatric building at Bossangoa hospital
cf.dek: The facility is designed for seasonal surges in child malaria and malnutrition cases that begin as early as July.
paragraphs: Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF), working with the Central African Republic’s health ministry, has built a 52-bed paediatric building at the regional university hospital in Bossangoa, in the country’s north. The 343-square-metre facility, called “Pic”, was built to handle rising child malaria and malnutrition cases during the rainy season.

MSF nursing-care manager Jean-Paul Kikwayabo said 80% of malnourished patients at the hospital also have malaria. The illnesses often peak in July and August, when rains bring more mosquitoes and farm families’ food reserves are depleted after planting. The new building is intended to ease pressure on paediatric services and improve care.

Ornella, a market vegetable seller whose young son had malnutrition and signs of malaria, said hospital staff gave him medicines, milk and Plumpy’nut, a peanut-based nutrition paste. MSF gave the building to the hospital as a lasting investment in regional health services.

km.headline: Comoros official urges stronger voice in international negotiations
km.dek: At MEDays 2026 in Tangier, Nour El-Fath Azali said island states need stronger institutions, skills and political will to advance their interests.
paragraphs: Nour El-Fath Azali, Comoros’ secretary-general of government, called for the country to have more influence in international negotiations at MEDays 2026 in Tangier, Morocco. He spoke on a panel titled “From the periphery to the decision-making table.”

Azali said island states often receive international decisions rather than help shape them. He argued that geography and resources can give them advantages, but that institutions, expertise and political will are needed to use those assets when their interests are at stake.

He described sovereignty as the ability to make national rules, control resources and enforce decisions. Drawing on Morocco’s institutional experience, he also discussed Mayotte and Western Sahara, while distinguishing the two cases and stressing the need for a coherent national strategy and institutions able to sustain it.

cg.headline: Congo steps up price checks and eases diesel access for essential-goods suppliers
cg.dek: Inspections from 25 October to 14 November found breaches of approved prices as the government works to restore a reference price for butane gas.
paragraphs: The Republic of Congo’s government has stepped up price surveillance and eased access to diesel for operators supplying essential goods, following inspections that found pricing irregularities. The measures were discussed at a cabinet meeting, alongside anti-corruption work and plans to modernise public administration.

Trade Minister Jacqueline Lydia Mikolo said checks from 25 October to 14 November found sellers charging above approved prices and some imported goods without approved prices. The government is revising the order governing butane-gas prices to restore a reference tariff that operators must follow.

The cabinet called for continued monitoring of prices, quality and availability, and action against speculation and the withholding of goods. The government also discussed preparations for Congo’s next anti-corruption evaluation, scheduled for 2027.

cg.headline: Congo approves bills for 2063 vision and five-year development plan
cg.dek: The proposals set out six development pillars and public investment plans, and now go to Parliament for examination and adoption.
paragraphs: The Republic of Congo’s government approved bills for a long-term development vision through 2063 and a five-year national plan for 2027-2031 at a cabinet meeting. The proposals will be sent to Parliament for examination and adoption.

Economy and Planning Minister Ludovic Ngatsé presented the bills. The vision centres on developing transport, logistics and services, alongside processing raw materials locally. Its six pillars include energy, digital services, infrastructure, industry, mining, hydrocarbons and agriculture. The 2027-2031 plan includes governance, human capital, energy, infrastructure, resource development and social protection, supported by a public investment programme and monitoring system.

The cabinet also approved an investment charter bill to improve legal protections for investors and credit access for small and medium-sized businesses. It adopted a decree to update national accounts using the 2008 system, with the aim of better measuring informal activity, natural resources and digital services.

cg.headline: Congo ministers consider law to set development vision through 2063
cg.dek: The proposed framework would put long-term national development priorities into law and guide successive plans, the economy minister said.
paragraphs: The Republic of Congo’s Council of Ministers considered a bill on Wednesday, 25 November, to approve Vision Congo 2063, a long-term framework for national development. The meeting was held at the People’s Palace under President Denis Sassou N’Guesso.

Economy Minister Ludovic Ngatsé said the vision would set development orientations through 2063 and establish their continuity in law. Successive national development plans would carry out the framework progressively, according to the minister’s presentation.
The proposal is the national component of the African Union’s Agenda 2063. The council also had three other bills, one draft decree, four ministerial communications and appointments on its agenda.

cg.headline: Congo launches two projects for livestock health and seed production
cg.dek: The animal-health programme funds equipment for Brazzaville’s laboratory and nine control points, while a second project targets maize and forage seeds.
paragraphs: The Republic of Congo’s agriculture and livestock ministry, with support from the United Nations Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO), launched two projects in Brazzaville last weekend to strengthen farming and livestock. One focuses on animal health; the other aims to expand production of maize and forage-plant seeds.

The animal-health project has funding of 250 000 US dollars and runs from August 2026 to 2028, the ministry said. It will equip Brazzaville’s laboratory and provide materials to nine control points for collecting, preserving and transporting samples. 60 agents are to be trained, with work also planned at abattoirs in Brazzaville and Pointe-Noire.

The seed project covers the Plateaux, Bouenza and Cuvette departments. It will organise production from basic seed multiplication through producer cooperatives, under the supervision of the National Centre for Improved Seeds.

ci.headline: Ivory Coast replaces 14 BTS fields with 16 new specialities
ci.dek: The cabinet approved the overhaul in Abidjan, adding courses including cybersecurity and energy efficiency while modernising 19 existing fields.
paragraphs: Ivory Coast’s cabinet approved a reform of the Higher Technician Certificate (BTS) on Wednesday, 25 November, in Abidjan. The changes remove 14 of the diploma’s 33 fields, modernise 19 and add 16 specialities, bringing the total to 35.

The higher-education ministry said the discontinued fields no longer offered job prospects. The new options include cybersecurity, energy efficiency, digital systems maintenance and metal-structure construction. Employers’ representatives from 13 professional branches approved the programmes, which will place more emphasis on practical training.

The ministry has not set a start date or explained what happens to students already enrolled in fields being removed. It is also expected to provide an adaptation timetable for colleges offering the diploma.

ci.headline: Ivory Coast suspends influencer’s driving licence for four years
ci.dek: The influencer admitted speeding at 120 km/h on a road limited to 100 km/h, and must return to driving school before regaining his licence.
paragraphs: Ivory Coast’s driving-licence commission suspended influencer and web comedian Amany Kouakou Florent, known as Observateur Ébène, for four years at a hearing in Abidjan on Thursday, 26 November 2026. The decision followed several alleged traffic offences, including speeding on the Abidjan-Mondoukou road.

The commission said Florent admitted driving at 120 km/h where the limit was 100 km/h. His record also showed unpaid fines totalling more than 600 CFA000. After the suspension, he must complete training at a driving school before he can obtain a licence again. As he lives in France, authorities will inform him of the ruling through France’s embassy.

The commission reviewed 43 cases in the session and imposed 32 licence sanctions. Oumar Sacko, director general of land transport and traffic, said enforcement must follow procedure and protect road users.

paragraphs: A court in Abidjan postponed a case involving alleged illegal gold mining and money laundering in the classified Songan forest, near Bettié, to 10 December 2026. Lieutenant Z. S. Herbert Melaine, a local forestry agency unit chief, admitted setting amounts of money in exchange for releasing people detained in the forest.

The economic and financial criminal court was hearing charges against 12 people. Melaine said his team worked without weapons and lacked equipment and funds. A co-defendant, the president of Bettié’s youth group, said Melaine asked him to contact detainees’ families after arrests. The defendants are presumed innocent.
The hearing was adjourned because two defendants speak English and no interpreter was present. Melaine had been released provisionally on 16 June 2026.

eg.headline: Maersk plans full Suez Canal service return by March 2027
eg.dek: The carrier has resumed canal and Red Sea operations, while its CEO says the rest of its network will return over coming months.
paragraphs: Maersk plans to restore its full shipping network through Egypt’s Suez Canal over the coming months, as regional security improves. Chief Executive Vincent Clerc told President Abdel Fattah El-Sisi that the canal remained Maersk’s preferred route and the company had resumed operations through it and the Red Sea.

In October, the Denmark-based carrier expected all its services to transit the canal again by March 2027. Maersk-affiliated vessels made 276 canal transits from January to September 2026, carrying 23.3 million net tons, up from 146 transits and 7 million net tons in the same period of 2025, Suez Canal Authority figures show.

Clerc also outlined plans to increase vessel capacity and expand the fleet. Separately, Scatec CEO Terje Pilskog said the company plans to invest about US$5 billion in Egypt over the next two years in renewable energy, desalination, green data centres and related infrastructure.

eg.headline: Egypt and Chevron review steps to link Cyprus gas field to Egyptian infrastructure
eg.dek: A joint workshop examined the Aphrodite project’s regulatory requirements, facility assessments and process-safety measures.
paragraphs: Egypt’s petroleum ministry and Chevron reviewed development plans for Cyprus’ Aphrodite natural gas field and its planned connection to Egypt’s infrastructure at a joint workshop. The meeting, held under Petroleum Minister Karim Badawi’s auspices, also covered technical and regulatory requirements.

The ministry said on Wednesday, November 25, that participants examined the project’s current status and requirements for classifying major-hazard facilities, supporting technical assessments and submitting notifications to regulators. They identified next steps and coordination arrangements for the two sides’ working teams to complete the procedures.

Discussion also covered process-safety systems, equipment maintenance and occupational health, safety and environmental standards. Chevron’s Cyprus country manager, Basel Allam, said the company applies international practices to assess and manage risks to facilities, equipment, workers and the surrounding environment.

eg.headline: Egypt signs Greece business pact and Jordan aviation agreement
eg.dek: The Greece deal covers nine sectors, while the Jordan agreement seeks to expand air links and give airlines more operating opportunities.
paragraphs: Egypt signed two agreements in November: a business cooperation memorandum with Greece on 21 November in Athens, and an aviation memorandum with Jordan on the sidelines of a Montreal conference. The Egyptian Junior Business Association and the Athens Chamber of Commerce and Industry signed the Greece deal, which covers nine sectors.

The Greece agreement provides for trade missions, business meetings, sector forums and exchanges of economic information to help companies find partners. The aviation agreement, initialled by Egypt and Jordan, is intended to improve coordination between their authorities, update air transport regulations and support passenger travel, tourism and trade.

Bilateral merchandise trade between Egypt and Greece reached €1.45 billion in 2025, according to the Athens chamber. Jordan was Egypt’s third-largest individual market for processed food exports in the first eight months of 2026, with sales of US$228 million, Egypt’s Food Export Council reported.

gq.headline: Equatorial Guinea's lawmakers adopt report urging CEMAC states to pay dues
gq.dek: The report says some members failed to pay the bloc's main revenue levy in 2025, hampering its institutions and community projects.
paragraphs: Equatorial Guinea's Chamber of Deputies adopted a report on the Central African Economic and Monetary Community (CEMAC) on Wednesday, 25 November. The document reviews the regional parliament's ordinary session, held in Malabo from 2 February to 3 March 2026, and says funding shortfalls and unpaid member-state contributions obstruct the bloc's work.

Crispín Engono Nguema, the community deputy who presented the report, said some states did not pay the Community Integration Tax in 2025. The levy is CEMAC's main revenue source, and the shortfall hampers regional projects and institutional operations. Community representatives agreed to run a campaign urging member states to pay their contributions.

The report also cites incomplete reforms, reliance on oil and difficulties completing regional integration. The assembly unanimously backed a resolution on fully implementing decisions of the Central African Economic Union's Council of Ministers.

gq.headline: Equatorial Guinea Senate president proposes rules for traditional marriage
gq.dek: Teresa Efua Asangono says wedding expenses are delaying formal unions and pushing many couples into cohabitation.
paragraphs: Equatorial Guinea’s Senate president, Teresa Efua Asangono, has proposed a legal framework to regulate customary marriage, saying high wedding costs are delaying formal unions and pushing numerous couples into cohabitation. She presented the proposal during parliamentary debates on social cohesion and family protection.

Asangono said the absence of rules on bride price and ceremonies allows arbitrary demands and leaves both partners without legal protection. She said women in traditional unions without civil marriage face particular vulnerability in separation, inheritance and widowhood, while young men with low incomes or no jobs can be unable to afford formal marriage.

She cited costs including venue and equipment rentals, catering, more than 300 uniform outfits, conditional lists of appliances, vehicles or homes, and payments called “hotel” and “ewonga” in Fang. Asangono said her proposal would regulate tradition, not legislate against it.

The symbolic handover of the keys took place between the university's rector, Filiberto Ntutumu Nguema Nchama, and the deputy education minister in charge of school and sports infrastructure, Constantino Obiang Esono Ayingono.

The building will house the Centro 12 de Octubre, which until now has operated in the Ela Nguema district. The new site will provide suitable space for its students, teachers and administrative staff, and is expected to improve the conditions in which its technical and vocational training programmes are taught. The property became available after the university reorganised its spaces and moved the activities based there to other campuses.
The handover will also make it possible to set up laboratories in the future to strengthen the practical training of students.

gq.headline: Equatorial Guinea vice-president seeks stricter Miss selection rules
gq.dek: Teodoro Nguema Obiang Mangue says candidates at home and abroad should have equal opportunities while demonstrating knowledge of the country.
paragraphs: Equatorial Guinea Vice-President Teodoro Nguema Obiang Mangue has proposed stricter rules for selecting the country’s Miss contestants, calling for a more transparent and equitable process. He said the rules should give young women living in Equatorial Guinea and those abroad equal opportunities.

Nguema Obiang Mangue said the proposal would not exclude candidates abroad, but would require all contestants to know the country’s culture, customs, social realities and challenges. He questioned whether a contestant who arrives one or two months before the pageant can fairly represent the country internationally, saying residents who experience daily life there may be disadvantaged.
He said beauty and talent should be accompanied by knowledge, identity and commitment to the nation. The proposal concerns the selection system; the reports gave no timetable for changing it.

er.headline: Abiy says Eritrea rejected power, road and port offers as tensions grow
er.dek: Ethiopia's prime minister accuses Asmara of arming forces hostile to Ethiopia and warns that destruction will fall upon Eritrea if it does not change course.
paragraphs: Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed accused Eritrea of arming forces hostile to Ethiopia and warned of grave consequences if Asmara did not change course. Speaking to parliament on November 26, he set two conditions for peaceful coexistence: that Eritrea stop arming and collaborating with those forces, and that it join joint development, with Ethiopia contributing the ideas, the money and the labour.

The state-run Ethiopian News Agency reported that Ethiopia had offered Eritrea electricity at Ethiopian domestic tariffs and proposed joint road and port projects, and that Eritrea had rejected the initiatives. Abiy said relations deteriorated after Eritrean forces entered Tigray during the 2020-22 war, accusing them of killing young people, destroying infrastructure and looting property.

Eight days earlier, Reuters reported that the two sides had massed forces along their shared border, bringing the armies within striking distance of each other. Eritrean Information Minister Yemane Gebremeskel dismissed the reports as propaganda.

ke.headline: Kenyan court bars Ebola centre work and orders US deal disclosure
ke.dek: Justice Patricia Nyaundi ruled that the government breached the Constitution by allowing the 50-bed facility to be built without public participation.
paragraphs: A Kenyan court on Thursday ruled that the government breached the Constitution by allowing construction of a US-backed Ebola quarantine centre at a military base in Laikipia without public participation. Justice Patricia Nyaundi barred further construction and operations at the 50-bed facility and ordered the government to disclose all agreements with the United States within 45 days.

The facility prompted deadly protests by residents who feared exposure to Ebola and pressure on Kenya's health system. The case was brought by the Law Society of Kenya and Katiba Institute, a constitutional watchdog; in May, the High Court had ordered work stopped while it considered their petition.

The US had planned to commit $13.5 million to Kenya's Ebola preparedness efforts. Kenya reported nine Ebola cases after its first case in October, all involving direct contacts of the initial patient.

ke.headline: Kenya elects five sugar growers to board seats
ke.dek: The representatives were chosen by 108,372 registered growers, and will serve three-year terms after the agriculture secretary gazettes their names.
paragraphs: Five sugar farmers were elected to represent growers on the Kenya Sugar Board in nationwide votes across the country’s five sugar-growing regions on November 24. Each region elected one representative, and 108,372 registered growers voted, a turnout of 43.9%.

The Elections Committee said it had sent the successful candidates’ names to the Cabinet Secretary for Agriculture and Livestock Development for gazettement. Once gazetted, they will serve as board directors for three years. The board is expected to oversee the Sugar Act 2024 and monitor millers, with a focus on timely farmer payments and sugar production.

Kenya is projected to produce 900,000 metric tonnes of sugar in 2026, against estimated annual demand of 1.0 million to 1.2 million tonnes, leaving a projected deficit of about 100,000 to 300,000 tonnes.

ke.headline: Ruto and Mnangagwa open presidential commission on Kenya-Zimbabwe ties
ke.dek: The leaders are due to review existing agreements and trade barriers, with Kenya targeting US$70 million in annual bilateral trade.
paragraphs: Zimbabwean President Emmerson Mnangagwa began a two-day state visit to Kenya on Friday with a ceremonial 21-gun salute at State House in Nairobi. He inspected a guard of honour before talks with Kenyan President William Ruto.

The presidents are scheduled to co-chair the first Zimbabwe-Kenya Bi-National Commission, elevating cooperation from a joint permanent commission to presidential-level engagement. The commission is expected to review commitments and identify economic opportunities, as the two governments seek to ease cross-border trade barriers and increase private-sector participation.

Kenya and Zimbabwe have signed 17 bilateral agreements covering areas including agriculture, investment promotion, transport and education. Further agreements are expected to be considered during the commission.

za.headline: Western Cape court voids report behind Ramaphosa impeachment proceedings
za.dek: A unanimous ruling also set aside Parliament’s steps based on the report, while the African Transformation Movement weighs an appeal.
paragraphs: South Africa’s Western Cape High Court on Wednesday, 25 November, set aside the report that had opened the way for impeachment proceedings against President Cyril Ramaphosa. A full bench ruled unanimously that the independent panel report was unlawful and also nullified the subsequent steps Parliament took on its basis.

The judges found that the panel, chaired by former chief justice Sandile Ngcobo, used the wrong evidentiary test and went beyond the allegations Ramaphosa had been asked to answer. The panel’s November 2022 report said he had a case to answer over $580 000 stolen from his Phala Phala farm in February 2020. The court did not decide the underlying misconduct allegations.

Impeachment Committee chair Makashule Gana said it had sought legal advice on whether its meeting scheduled for 26 November could go ahead. Speaker Thoko Didiza will study the judgment, and the African Transformation Movement is consulting lawyers about a possible appeal.

za.headline: South African public schools expect fee increases of up to 10% in 2027
za.dek: Fedsas says some schools are forecasting increases of 12% to 15%, as families already cut grocery spending and use savings to pay education costs.
paragraphs: Fees at many fee-charging public schools in South Africa are expected to rise by 7% to 10% in 2027, putting added pressure on families already reducing grocery spending and dipping into savings to keep children in class. Uniforms, stationery, transport and meal costs can also fall due in the same month as school fees.

Riaan van der Bergh, deputy chief executive of the Federation of Governing Bodies of South African Schools (Fedsas), said schools it had consulted expected increases in that range, while some outliers planned hikes of 12% to 15%. He expects more parents to seek fee exemptions in 2027; some have already said during admissions that they intend to apply for relief.

Public primary fees rose 6% from 2025 to 2026, while secondary fees increased 5.7%, according to the Competition Commission. Fedsas says school expenses such as salaries, municipal rates, electricity and water rise faster than headline inflation, squeezing budgets for textbooks, learning support and upkeep.

paragraphs: ActionSA’s Nasiphi Moya won election as executive mayor of the City of Tshwane on Thursday, 26 November, securing 115 votes in the council’s inaugural meeting. DA candidate Cilliers Brink received 87 votes.

za.headline: South Africa braces for storms before a drier El Niño summer
za.dek: Forecasters say thunderstorms are due over the Free State and Gauteng, and temperatures will climb to 32ºC-36ºC once the cloud over the interior clears.
paragraphs: Heavy rain, hail and severe thunderstorms have struck many parts of the country as El Niño takes hold. South African Weather Service senior forecaster Tokelo Chiloane said temperatures are set to rise once cloud over the interior breaks, mostly staying between 32ºC and 36ºC.

Weather forecaster Juandre Vorster said the storms were caused by the El Niño effect and that another round is expected over the Free State and Gauteng. Michelle du Plessis of Vox said the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration expects the strong-to-very strong event to last through January to March.

Du Plessis said the South African Weather Service's outlook shows a higher chance of below-normal rain across large parts of the summer rainfall region from November to March. She said climate models still predict the event will peak in December or January.

za.headline: Durban remains South Africa's cheapest metro for buying property
za.dek: Outside the city centre, the average home there sells for R920 000, while Johannesburg's average is R1.1 million, according to a property report.
paragraphs: Durban is the cheapest metro in South Africa to buy property outside the city centre, where the average sale price is R920 000, according to The South African. Johannesburg's average sale price across the rest of the city is R1.1 million, while flats in Cape Town's central business district cost upwards of R1 million.

In Durban's city centre, the average sale price is R420 000, and a studio flat needs at least R280 000. Statistics South Africa puts the expanded unemployment rate in eThekwini, the municipality that includes Durban, at 39.2% as of the third quarter. Property prices in Durban rose 5.1% between 2021 and 2025.
In Pretoria, the average sale price in the broader city is R989 000, up 16.8% over five years. The report says Johannesburg's average price outside the centre was unchanged from 2024.

ng.headline: Oyedele urges Nigerian firms to compete under AfCFTA
ng.dek: The finance minister says access to African markets will bring prosperity only if businesses produce competitively and diversify exports.
paragraphs: Nigeria’s Finance Minister Taiwo Oyedele called using the African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA) to boost exports and diversify the economy an urgent national task at a forum in Abuja on Thursday. He said Nigeria must produce more competitively, earn more from its output and create better opportunities for Nigerians.

Abba Bello, head of the Nigeria Export-Import Bank, said the country must process more of its products to compete and earn more foreign exchange. He said many exports remain raw while Nigeria imports finished goods, citing cocoa and chocolate, cotton and textiles, and hide and skin and leather products.

Bello called for more manufactured and value-added exports and stronger value chains in agriculture and solid minerals. Tope Fashua, an economic adviser to the president, said Africa could no longer serve as a raw-materials warehouse for the rest of the world.

ng.headline: Fashola says Tinubu's identity questions resurface before elections
ng.dek: The former Lagos governor says Tinubu met the constitutional requirements to contest and predicts he will win again in 2027.
paragraphs: Babatunde Fashola, a former Lagos State governor, said questions about President Bola Tinubu’s background and identity return whenever Tinubu is close to winning an election. Fashola made the remarks in an interview with ARISE News, saying the dispute had continued for more than two decades.

Fashola said Tinubu had met the constitutional requirements to run for president and that voters had already decided the issue. He cited Tinubu’s 2023 victory and said Nigerians would reaffirm their position in 2027. He also said parts of the dispute had been litigated in 1999 and during the last presidential election, and that a House investigation took place in 1999.
Fashola urged opposition politicians to focus on issues that improve people’s lives rather than repeatedly raising questions about Tinubu’s identity.

ng.headline: Nigeria and IFAD review SAPZ delivery ahead of mid-term review
ng.dek: The mission is assessing implementation in Ogun and Kano, where the programme targets 100,000 direct and 500,000 indirect beneficiaries.
paragraphs: Nigeria’s Federal Government and the International Fund for Agricultural Development (IFAD) began a joint review of the Special Agro-Industrial Processing Zones (SAPZ) programme in Abuja on 24 November, ahead of its first additional financing and mid-term review. The mission is intended to speed up delivery and address bottlenecks.

Dr. Emmanuel Oladipo Akogun, a director in the Federal Ministry of Agriculture and Food Security, said the review would examine activities, contracts, disbursements and results. The programme supports rice and cassava value chains in Ogun and Kano, with targets of 100,000 direct and 500,000 indirect beneficiaries, particularly women and young people. In Kano, a 2024 pilot supported more than 1,000 smallholder farmers and farmer organisations.

Field visits are scheduled from 25 November to 2 December. The mission will produce a supervision report and recommendations; the initial loan period runs until 30 September 2029, with financial closure set for 31 March 2030.

ng.headline: Nigeria's agency and AGRA target $25m for farm-business financing
ng.dek: AGRA has committed an initial $100,000 to a facility meant to make professional business support more affordable for agribusinesses.
paragraphs: The Alliance for a Green Revolution in Africa (AGRA) and the Small and Medium Enterprises Development Agency of Nigeria (SMEDAN) are targeting at least $25m in financing for agricultural small and medium-sized enterprises. They are also backing a support facility to strengthen the businesses' capacity.

AGRA has committed an initial $100,000 to a Multi-Donor Business Development Services Cost-Sharing Facility, which will pool resources from development partners, financial institutions and government agencies. Dr Godswill Aguiyi, representing AGRA Nigeria Country Director Rufus Idris, said many agribusinesses struggle to attract investors because of poor financial records, weak corporate governance, limited technology adoption and inadequate market intelligence.

The initiative, unveiled at a two-day Agribusiness Network Meeting in Ibadan, Oyo State, also seeks to improve links between businesses, buyers and financial institutions. Dr Stanley Ibeku of the Enterprise Development Centre at Pan-Atlantic University said financial literacy, management skills, investment readiness and access to viable markets are essential alongside training and loans.

et.headline: Ethiopia commits $342.4 million to equip 120 health facilities
et.dek: The three-year maternal and child health programme combines a $20 million foundation pledge with partner funding matched by the government.
paragraphs: Ethiopia will equip around 120 health facilities with medicines, medical equipment and lifesaving technologies over three years under a $342.4 million reproductive, maternal, newborn and child health programme. The funding is intended to improve care across the country, particularly for pregnant women, newborns and children.

Health Minister Mekdes Daba said the foundation's $20 million pledge to Ethiopia's health compact helped mobilize another $151.2 million from development partners, which the government matched. Planned purchases include artificial intelligence-enabled ultrasound equipment to help staff identify pregnancy complications, as well as antibiotics to reduce infection risks, including sepsis.

The wider initiative, announced by the Mohamed bin Zayed Foundation for Humanity at a public health conference in Addis Ababa, is expected to benefit more than 500 facilities in nine African countries. The foundation said its $135 million commitment is expected to attract more than $550 million in further financing.

et.headline: Ethiopia’s out-of-school children reach 4.2 million
et.dek: A 2026 African Child Policy Forum report says conflict disrupted education as social protection reached only 11.5% of Ethiopians.
paragraphs: The African Child Policy Forum’s 2026 report estimates that 4.2 million primary-school-age children in Ethiopia were out of school in 2024, up from 1.8 million in 2017. The report links the increase to conflict disrupting children’s education.

Only 11.5% of Ethiopians, according to the report, receive at least one social protection benefit, so most people have little cover against economic shocks. Poverty, rising living costs and inadequate public support are, it says, eroding family wellbeing across the continent.

Governments should widen family benefits and cash transfers, shield social protection budgets from cuts and make public spending more accountable, the forum recommends. The eighth edition of its flagship report draws on continental data and case studies from Cameroon, Ghana, Morocco, Tanzania and Zimbabwe.

et.headline: Abiy says El Niño caused less than 1% disruption to Ethiopia
et.dek: The prime minister told parliament that advance crop, fodder and water measures helped avert a nationwide agricultural and humanitarian emergency.
paragraphs: Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed told Ethiopia’s House of Peoples Representatives on Thursday that El Niño caused less than 1% macroeconomic and agricultural disruption. He said the country had passed the weather event’s most critical phase after early forecasts warned of drought conditions comparable to the 2015–2016 crisis.

Abiy credited early warnings, water infrastructure and preventive farm measures, including distributing fast-maturing, drought-tolerant seeds and expanding fodder production. He said western Ethiopia received abundant rain, while several lowland corridors faced moisture deficits, reduced yields, depleted pasture and local water shortages.

Federal agencies remain on high alert, Abiy said. Independent humanitarian and climate assessments report continuing agricultural strain in some areas and growing flood hazards in the final weeks of the year.

gh.headline: Terkper urges Ghana to resist fresh borrowing after debt defaults
gh.dek: The former finance minister says the Heavily Indebted Poor Countries (HIPC) initiative, later defaults and the domestic debt exchange should keep successive governments.
paragraphs: Former Finance Minister Seth Terkper urged Ghana's successive governments to maintain fiscal discipline and avoid unsustainable borrowing, speaking on JoyNews' PM Express on Thursday, November 26. He was discussing the 2027 Budget and said the country should not repeat the borrowing practices that led to its debt crisis.

Terkper said the experience of the Heavily Indebted Poor Countries (HIPC) initiative, later debt defaults and the Domestic Debt Exchange Programme should serve as a lasting warning. He also backed the Cedi Sinking Fund, which sets aside money for debt repayments, and said planned bond buybacks could help restore investor confidence. Finance Minister Cassiel Ato Forson said the fund held GH¢29 billion as of November 11, enough to cover principal on domestic bonds due in February 2027.

The budget plans monthly transfers equal to seven per cent of gross domestic non-oil tax revenue into the fund, alongside targeted domestic bond issuances. The government has said it plans to settle the February obligation ahead of schedule.

gh.headline: Ghana's iron and steel corporation plans regulations for Parliament within three months
gh.dek: The proposed legislative instrument would cover mining, steel processing plants and the scrap metal trade, and the corporation says consultations are in their final stages.
paragraphs: The Ghana Integrated Iron and Steel Development Corporation (GIISDEC) is targeting the submission of a proposed legislative instrument to Parliament within the next two to three months to regulate the country's iron and steel industry. The rules are expected to set guidelines for the upstream, midstream and downstream segments, including the scrap metal sector.

Chief Executive William Okofo Dartey disclosed the plan at a stakeholders' consultation forum in Accra on Thursday, November 26, 2026. He said the consultation is meant to operationalise the Ghana Integrated Iron and Steel Development Corporation Act, 2019 (Act 988), and to gather contributions from industry players and government agencies before the instrument is finalised. Mr Dartey said the midstream framework would guide the establishment and operation of steel processing plants, promoting local value addition, as Ghana currently imports significant quantities of raw materials, including steel slabs.

Mr Dartey said the corporation had held stakeholder engagements over the past year with traditional authorities, district assemblies and communities in areas with iron ore deposits, including the Shieni deposit in the Tatale-Zabzugu District. He said the corporation was in the final stages of consultations.

gh.headline: Powered by Africa plans $100 million real estate fund for diaspora investors
gh.dek: The platform launched in Accra after a five-day gathering that drew delegates from 27 African countries and beyond.
paragraphs: Powered by Africa, a new international platform, has been launched in Accra to draw global capital and diaspora money into African infrastructure. Its next major step is a proposed $100 million real estate fund aimed at diaspora and international investors.

The launch follows the platform's inaugural 2026 gathering, held from November 17 to 21, where more than 300 political leaders, investors, executives and diaspora figures met. Founder and campaign director Samuel Kasumu said the group would tell Africa's stories while bringing people together to show what the continent is building.

The platform also intends to set up an infrastructure council led by prominent African business leaders and to hold a major event in New York during the 2027 United Nations General Assembly. On November 20 it unveiled Powered by Africa 100, a list of 100 people driving infrastructure and industrial development across the continent.

tz.headline: Tanzania signs €175 million French loans for water, food and dairy
tz.dek: The agreements allocate €90 million to Lake Victoria water and sanitation, €55 million to food infrastructure and €30 million to smallholder dairy.
paragraphs: Tanzania signed three concessional loan agreements worth €175 million with the French Development Agency in Paris on November 24, to fund water and sanitation, urban food infrastructure and dairy projects. The agreements were signed by Finance Minister Khamis Mussa Omar and the agency’s chief executive, Christophe Lecourtier.

The largest loan, €90 million, will fund the second phase of the Lake Victoria Water and Sanitation Project for communities around the lake. A €55 million loan will support food-trade and distribution infrastructure in Mwanza and Tanga. The remaining €30 million will finance a programme for smallholder dairy farmers across Tanzania, co-financed with the International Fund for Agricultural Development, to improve milk production and climate adaptation.

The Ministry of Foreign Affairs and East African Cooperation said the agreements bring Tanzania’s total development cooperation with the agency to €1.3 billion. The water project and urban food programme are also expected to receive European Union grants administered by the agency.

Tanzania signed three concessional loan agreements worth €175 million with the French Development Agency in Paris on November 24, to fund water and sanitation, urban food infrastructure and dairy projects. The agreements were signed by Finance Minister Khamis Mussa Omar and the agency’s chief executive, Christophe Lecourtier.

The largest loan, €90 million, will fund the second phase of the Lake Victoria Water and Sanitation Project for communities around the lake. A €55 million loan will support food-trade and distribution infrastructure in Mwanza and Tanga. The remaining €30 million will finance a programme for smallholder dairy farmers across Tanzania, co-financed with the International Fund for Agricultural Development, to improve milk production and climate adaptation.

The Ministry of Foreign Affairs and East African Cooperation said the agreements bring Tanzania’s total development cooperation with the agency to €1.3 billion. The water project and urban food programme are also expected to receive European Union grants administered by the agency.

tz.headline: Tanzania secures US$85 million for maternal and newborn care
tz.dek: The five-year Beginnings Fund partnership will support 210 mainland facilities and allocate US$9.6 million to Zanzibar.
paragraphs: Tanzania has announced a five-year US$85 million partnership with the Beginnings Fund to improve maternal and newborn care, as President Samia Suluhu Hassan called for stronger regional accountability. The announcement came at a reproductive, maternal, newborn, child and adolescent health conference in Dar es Salaam on November 26, 2026.

Beginnings Fund chief executive Alice Kang’ethe said US$75.4 million would go to mainland Tanzania, supporting 210 high-volume facilities and aiming to reach about 7.3 million women and newborns. Funding will cover health workers, equipment, medicines and delivery systems, with implementation led by the government through the Health Ministry and the Prime Minister’s Office.

The government also launched a 2026–2030 health plan and a mortality report. Samia said maternal deaths in 2024/25 stood at 76 per 100,000 live births; newborn mortality was 17 per 1,000, and under-five mortality was 28 per 1,000.

tz.headline: Tadokoro urges Tanzania and Japan to protect open sea routes
tz.dek: The Japanese scholar said prosperity depends on rules that safeguard smaller countries as well as restraining powerful ones.
paragraphs: Japanese international relations scholar Masayuki Tadokoro urged Tanzania and Japan to cooperate on protecting open sea routes and international rules at a public lecture in Dar es Salaam on November 24, 2026. He argued that economic prosperity depends on an order that protects smaller countries while restraining powerful ones.

Tadokoro, a professor at the International University of Japan and professor emeritus at Keio University, linked Japan’s post-war development to maritime trade security and Tanzania’s position on the Indian Ocean. His presentation said the concern was the erosion of rules, not the rise of any country, and distinguished that concern from opposition to China’s economic development.
Japan announced an updated Free and Open Indo-Pacific policy on May 2, which it seeks to turn into cooperation on supply chains, digital infrastructure, growth and security.

ma.headline: EU caps Moroccan hybrid imports at 23,954 vehicles for 200 days
ma.dek: The quota starts on December 1, after EU imports from Morocco reached 61,259 vehicles in the 12 months to June 2026.
paragraphs: The European Union will limit hybrid vehicle imports from Morocco to 23,954 over a maximum of 200 days from December 1, under temporary quotas covering several exporters. The cap is far below the 61,259 vehicles the bloc imported from Morocco between July 2025 and June 2026.

The European Commission set the Moroccan allocation in three stages: 10,779 vehicles from December 1 to February 28, 11,019 from March 1 to May 31, and 2,156 from June 1 to June 18. The regulation cites Eurostat data for the import figures.

Morocco supplied about 37,771 hybrid passenger vehicles to the EU in calendar 2025. Its shipments rose from 18 in 2023 to 26,815 in 2024; during the investigation period, Morocco ranked seventh among EU suppliers.

ma.headline: Laprophan raises 2,2 billion dirhams in Casablanca listing
ma.dek: The Moroccan pharmaceutical group drew demand of 15,2 billion dirhams from 44 378 investors, nearly seven times the amount offered.
paragraphs: Moroccan pharmaceutical group Laprophan began trading on the Casablanca Stock Exchange on Wednesday 25 November after an initial public offering priced at 341 dirhams per share. The offer raised 2,2 billion dirhams.

The subscription rate reached 6,89 times, with 44 378 investors taking part and demand totalling 15,2 billion dirhams, according to Maroc Diplomatique. The offer combined 4 105 500 newly issued shares with 2 412 200 existing shares sold by current holders.
Laprophan is the largest offering by a pharmaceutical company on the exchange, according to the same reports.

The projects are 85% owned by London-listed Aterian and 15% by Paris-based Geology AI, a company that combines artificial intelligence with geological science to find metals including copper, lithium, nickel and rare earth elements.
