rw.headline: Rwanda's central bank lifts benchmark rate to 9.5%
rw.dek: The 75-basis-point increase follows October inflation of 19.5% and takes the rate to its highest level since 2009.
paragraphs: The National Bank of Rwanda raised its benchmark interest rate to 9.5% on November 26, lifting it from 8.75% after three months at that level. The 75-basis-point increase is the bank’s latest move to contain rising inflation.

The Consumer Price Index rose 19.5% year-on-year in October, up from 17.2% in September, the National Institute of Statistics of Rwanda reported. Food and non-alcoholic beverage prices climbed 28.9% over the year, while transport costs rose 22.4%. The central bank’s medium-term inflation target is 5%.
The higher benchmark rate is intended to influence borrowing costs, credit demand and spending; it can also make loans more expensive for businesses and households with variable-rate debt.
rw.body:
The National Bank of Rwanda raised its benchmark interest rate to 9.5% on November 26, lifting it from 8.75% after three months at that level. The 75-basis-point increase is the bank’s latest move to contain rising inflation.

paragraphs: Mobile Money Rwanda generated Rwf 141.2 billion in revenue in the first nine months of 2026, up 29.1%, while its active users rose 12% to 6.5 million and its merchant network grew to 720,069. Taarifa Rwanda reported the figures after an interview with chief executive Chantal Kagame.

Airtel's share rose from 13.2% in December 2025 to 15.6% in June 2026. Kagame told Taarifa Rwanda that the industry faces policy bottlenecks, complicated onboarding and the task of protecting customers from fraud.

rw.headline: Rwanda’s chief justice demands measurable results from justice institutions
rw.dek: Domitilla Mukantaganzwa urged closer coordination as Rwanda works to deliver on 249 human-rights recommendations it accepted in 2026.
paragraphs: Rwanda’s Chief Justice, Domitilla Mukantaganzwa, told justice institutions on Thursday, 26 November, to measure success by changes in people’s lives, not by policies adopted. She spoke at the opening of the 11th Justice, Reconciliation, Law and Order Sector peer-review and Universal Periodic Review retreat in Nyagatare.

Mukantaganzwa called for institutions to coordinate across investigations, prosecutions, court hearings, legal aid and enforcement, saying delays at one stage can weaken the rest. Rwanda’s Rule of Law score in the Rwanda Governance Scorecard rose to 85.47% in 2026 from 81.63% in 2025, a gain of 3.84 percentage points.

Rwanda accepted 249 of 286 recommendations at its fourth Universal Periodic Review, held in January, and took note of the other 37. The justice sector is also working toward halving case backlogs under the second National Strategy for Transformation.

rw.headline: Three Rwandan tea factories certify 2025 production as carbon neutral
rw.dek: Mulindi, Shagasha and Nshili Kivu recorded about 32,926 tonnes of carbon removals beyond assessed emissions, according to the certification.
paragraphs: Black tea produced in 2025 by Rwanda's Mulindi, Shagasha and Nshili Kivu factories has received independent carbon-neutrality certification, The Wood Foundation Africa announced on November 24. The certification applies only to that year's production, not to future output or the tea's entire journey to consumers.

The assessment counted 24,076 tonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent in emissions against approximately 57,002 tonnes of recognised removals, leaving removals about 32,926 tonnes higher. Earthood Services Limited issued the certificate on October 30, verifying the data against two international standards for carbon footprints and greenhouse-gas inventories: ISO 14068-1:2023 (the international standard for carbon neutrality) and ISO 14064-3:2019 (the standard for verifying greenhouse-gas claims). Recognised removals came from plantations and shade trees within the assessment's boundaries.

The factories received 33 million kilogrammes of green leaf from 14,000 smallholder farmers in 2025, valued at about $9 million, and produced 7.6 million kilogrammes of tea worth $19 million. Rwanda is working on a national tea-sector strategy focused on branding, market expansion and competitiveness.

st.headline: President's new government tests his push to expand presidential power
st.dek: A Tela Non commentary questions whether the president will apply the doctrine behind his January 2025 dismissal of Patrice Trovoada's government.
paragraphs: A Tela Non commentary says São Tomé and Príncipe's president is now forming a government backed in parliament by the Movement for Change-Party of Social Progress (MCI-PS) and the Party of Unity and Nation (PUN), after dismissing Patrice Trovoada's government in January 2025. The author argues the president's actions have suggested he wants a role in shaping and influencing government policy, beyond serving as an arbiter of state institutions.

The president cited what he called the government's inability to solve economic and social problems, institutional disloyalty by Trovoada, the prime minister's lengthy absences abroad and public dissatisfaction. The commentary says those reasons helped start a drive to "presidentialise" the political system, but questions whether the president will follow that approach in forming the new government.

The author also warns that expanding presidential influence could weaken parliament's oversight role, while arguing that the president's earlier move had appeared motivated by a desire to address poverty and poor governance.

st.headline: Owners of SOLIVAN ask court to overturn Angolan control of Rosema brewery
st.dek: The request was filed on 24 November, days after the new government took office, reopening a 20-year dispute over the brewery's management.
paragraphs: The owners of SOLIVAN, a São Tomé and Príncipe company that has fought for control of the Rosema beer business for 20 years, asked the Constitutional Court on 24 November to cancel the ruling that returned the factory's possession, management and control to RIDUX, an Angolan private company. The filing came just after the new government took office.

SOLIVAN's lawyer confirmed to the outlet Téla Nón that the request had been submitted and said the company would make a public statement on the case in the coming period. The brewery had earlier been managed by RIDUX until parliament's majority, led by the ADI party, and the MCI-PS-PUN coalition used an interpretive law in 2023 to restore it to SOLIVAN's control.

Parliament later repealed that interpretive law after the ADI split in 2024, and newly appointed Constitutional Court judges overturned the ruling that had favoured SOLIVAN, returning the brewery to RIDUX. The report says the two companies have contested control of Rosema for 20 years.

st.headline: São Tomé and Príncipe makes 26 November a national holiday
st.dek: The first holiday commemorates the Algiers Agreement, which set the course toward independence from Portugal.
paragraphs: São Tomé and Príncipe observed 26 November as a national holiday for the first time in 2026, commemorating the Algiers Agreement signed on 26 November 1974. The agreement set the course toward the archipelago’s independence from Portugal.

President Carlos Vila Nova said the agreement prepared the details for the country to become an independent state and called for the date to be a day of reflection. The holiday recalls the end of 504 years of Portuguese colonial rule and the independence proclaimed on 12 July 1975.

National Assembly President Nilda da Mata said the agreement also opened the way for the election of the first constituent assembly. Vila Nova made his remarks before departing for Malabo, Equatorial Guinea, to attend the 27th summit of the Economic Community of Central African States.

sn.headline: Dakar court sets 9 December ruling on CFA200 million claim
sn.dek: Mame Mbaye Niang wants the transfer of a 250-square-metre Keur Gorgui villa annulled so he can pursue the damages awarded against Ousmane Sonko.
paragraphs: A civil chamber of Dakar’s high court will rule on 9 December on former tourism minister Mame Mbaye Niang’s request to cancel the transfer of a villa in the Keur Gorgui district. Niang is seeking to recover CFA200 million in damages awarded in a separate criminal case involving Ousmane Sonko.

The dispute concerns a villa of about 250 square metres and whose name should appear on its leasehold rights. Niang says the property was transferred to Sonko’s family to prevent a possible seizure; Sonko opposes the request and wants the family’s registration to remain. The judge heard the case on 25 November after lawyers for both sides filed written arguments.
Niang is also asking for the leasehold to be registered in Sonko’s name, which would allow him to pursue recovery of the damages.

sn.headline: Oulampane mayor remains in serious condition after suspected arson
sn.dek: Sagar Coly was burned at his home in Diacounda on Thursday and transferred to Ziguinchor for specialised treatment.
paragraphs: Sagar Coly, mayor of Oulampane in Senegal’s Bignona department, was badly burned in a fire at his home in Diacounda early Thursday, 26 November. He was taken to Ziguinchor for specialised treatment, and his condition remained serious on Friday, Dakaractu reported.

Investigators suspect Coly’s first wife started the fire after locking him in a room. Neighbours heard his cries and helped get him out. She was detained at Bounkiling and placed in police custody; accounts differ on where she was held afterward.

The prosecutor at Ziguinchor’s regional court has asked investigators to hear witnesses and establish whether the fire was planned. Reports say Coly had recently married a Senegalese woman living in France; the alleged role of that marriage is under investigation.

sn.headline: Senegal's PUMA invests CFA560 million in Casamance schools
sn.dek: The new facilities are for pupils in villages where displaced families have returned, and form the programme's first phase of support.
paragraphs: Senegal's Programme for the Emergency Modernisation of Border Roads and Territories (PUMA) has invested CFA560 million in school infrastructure for villages in Casamance where displaced families have returned. The facilities were inaugurated during an evaluation tour across Ziguinchor, Sédhiou and Kolda regions.

PUMA national coordinator Ndèye Marieme Samb said the schools were an initial stage of support for returning residents. The programme has also built health posts in some localities. Samb said PUMA had completed 75% of a project valued at CFA6.4 billion.

Further planned work includes village electrification, improving access to isolated villages and economic activities for women and young people. PUMA also plans to continue helping residents obtain civil-status documents, working with the relevant services.

sl.headline: Sierra Leone's electricity and water regulator lifts revenue to NLE 7.4 million
sl.dek: The regulator, which licenses power and water firms, collected NLE 7.4 million from levies and licenses in 2024, up from NLE 2.3 million in 2023.
paragraphs: Sierra Leone's Electricity and Water Regulatory Commission (SLEWRC) recorded NLE 7.4 million in internal revenue from levies and licenses in 2024, up from NLE 2.3 million in 2023. The commission regulates electricity and water service providers, issuing, renewing, suspending and revoking their licenses, and sets the rates they may charge.

Deputy Director Sama Sandi told the Ministry of Finance's bilateral budget discussions that the commission received no ministry funding in either 2023 or 2024, despite budget allocations. In 2023 it carried out enforcement against 64 non-compliant water companies and reported that 80% of complaints were resolved within a week of receipt. For 2024 it developed a multi-year tariff model for solar mini-grids, which was about to be completed.

For 2025, Sandi submitted a budget of NLE 5,590.29 for 2025 to 2027. The commission's plans include strengthening its organisational capacity and rolling out a safety and warranty system for water products.

sl.headline: Sierra Leone assigns 28,838 personnel to December census
sl.dek: Statistics Sierra Leone says the nationwide count starts Dec. 1, after 30,085 applicants sat the final recruitment examination.
paragraphs: Statistics Sierra Leone plans to deploy 28,838 personnel for Sierra Leone’s 2026 Population and Housing Census, which begins Dec. 1. Statistician-General and Chief Census Officer Andrew Bob Johnny announced the figure at a press conference in Freetown on Nov. 25.

Deputy Statistician-General Lansana Kpewolo Kanneh said 31,352 applicants were shortlisted, 30,652 attended training and 30,085 took the final examination. Johnny said the agency had received 3,000 additional tablets after some training centres faced shortages, and was reviewing equipment allocations and field assignments. Supervisors will monitor progress and identify areas needing support.

The agency says digital tools will track enumerators in real time and use GPS to check their assigned locations. United Nations Population Fund representative Kunle Adeniyi said the census falls within the UN’s 2030 round, covering 2025 to 2034.

sl.headline: Sierra Leone charcoal trade cuts trees and sustains households
sl.dek: A burner says his family relies on the work, while the environmental agency warns that cutting economic trees threatens food security.
paragraphs: Charcoal burning supports households across Sierra Leone, including in Freetown and regional headquarters towns, but depends on cutting trees. Pa Alimamy, a 65-year-old burner who has worked in the trade for more than two decades, said his entire family relies on it for a livelihood.

Paul Lamin, the Environmental Protection Agency’s director of natural resource governance, said burners are cutting economic trees such as orange and mango trees. He warned that cleared land is exposed to climate change and that losing those trees threatens food security. Lamin also said trees take a long time to regrow, and acknowledged that people have few alternative energy sources.

The government’s National Energy Compact says 36% of the population has access to electricity and clean cooking access stands at 15%. A Food and Agricultural Organization report estimates wood energy, including fuel wood and charcoal, emits 1/2.4 GT of carbon dioxide equivalent per year, or 2-7% of total human-caused greenhouse gas emissions.

sl.headline: Engage Salone finds Sierra Leone councils score 29.8 out of 100
sl.dek: A survey of 1,489 people across six council areas found 60% said their council never consults communities.
paragraphs: Engage Salone, a group that researched decentralisation, reported that Sierra Leone’s local councils scored an average of 29.8 out of 100. Its study surveyed 1,489 people across six council areas and found that decentralisation remains incomplete more than two decades after elected councils returned in 2004.

60% of respondents said their councils never consult communities, and only 17% had attended a council meeting. The report identified inadequate funding, weak coordination with central government, limited institutional capacity and political interference as obstacles to local governance.

Despite those concerns, 55% of respondents supported giving councils more powers and increased funding. The report also raised concerns about women’s participation in community governance and council responses during emergencies, including flooding.

sl.headline: Sierra Leone's vice presidency has rarely led to the presidency
sl.dek: A political analyst argues that the office has often served party balancing rather than preparing its holders to succeed the president.
paragraphs: Sierra Leonean political analyst Foday M. Daboh argues that the vice presidency has rarely provided a route to the presidency. In an article published in February 2026, he says successive governments have used the office to balance regional, religious and ethnic interests, manage party blocs and reward loyalty.

Daboh points to Solomon Ekuma Berewa, who became the Sierra Leone People's Party candidate in 2007 after serving as vice president, but lost the presidential election to Ernest Bai Koroma. He also describes Victor Bockarie Foh's tenure as short and politically constrained, while Samuel Sam-Sumana was expelled from his party after becoming estranged from the president.
The article says no Sierra Leone vice president has been elected president. It does not identify a next step for the current vice president.

so.headline: Puntland’s Deni rejects president’s UAE interference charge
so.dek: The Puntland leader said Somalia’s divisions were created by Somalis, as a caretaker cabinet amended 23 election-law articles and eight party-law articles.
paragraphs: Puntland President Said Abdullahi Deni on Wednesday called Somali President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud’s accusation of United Arab Emirates interference “unfortunate” and said blaming outsiders embarrassed the country. Deni said Somalia’s fractures were created by Somalis and must be resolved by them.

His remarks followed a 24 November cabinet session that changed 23 articles of the National Elections Law and eight articles of the parties law. The amendments introduce closed party lists, under which voters choose parties and seats go to candidates ranked by those parties, and set a 10% national-vote threshold for national-party status.

The Supreme Court ruled on 5 November that parliament’s mandate ended on 14 April 2026 and the president’s term on 15 May 2026, limiting both branches and the cabinet to caretaker duties. The government rejected the ruling. Deni said Puntland would protect Somali governance and rally the public behind it.

ss.headline: South Sudan adviser says civil servants work unpaid for months or years
ss.dek: Joseph Ngere Paciko said workers continue to report for duty and cover daily expenses themselves despite prolonged salary delays.
paragraphs: South Sudan’s presidential adviser on governance, Joseph Ngere Paciko, said civil servants continue reporting to work despite going months or even years without salaries. He spoke on Wednesday, November 25, at the close of a two-day China-South Sudan Governance Roundtable in Juba.

Paciko said workers use their own money for daily expenses while they keep working. He contrasted their experience with neighbouring countries, saying three months without pay there would bring widespread unrest. He also cautioned that workers’ attendance did not mean they were satisfied with their circumstances.

Paciko said governance is a system of rules, processes and structures for directing and holding a group accountable, and that the principles apply in settings including families, churches and communities.

ss.headline: Kiir ends emergency rule in four South Sudan states
ss.dek: The order restores ordinary duties to state and national institutions, while an analyst says the emergency failed to stop violence.
paragraphs: President Salva Kiir ended the state of emergency in Lakes, Warrap, Western Bahr el Ghazal and Unity states with immediate effect on Thursday evening, according to an order broadcast by state-owned South Sudan Broadcasting Corporation. The exceptional measures had been imposed on July 29.

Boboya James Edimond, a policy analyst and head of the Institute of Social Policy and Research in South Sudan, said intercommunal violence, revenge killings and cattle raiding continued despite security deployments. He cited clashes in Lakes’ Rumbek Centre County that reportedly killed more than 100 people, and said conflict prevented some areas of Western Bahr el Ghazal from completing voter registration.

Kiir ordered national and state institutions to resume their ordinary constitutional and legal responsibilities. Security bodies and the four governors must carry out the order, while security forces remain tasked with protecting civilians and maintaining public order.

ss.dek: A woman identified as Nyawura said she walked to a health facility the morning after armed men raped her on her way home.

sd.headline: Sudan food prices rise 57.23% as households cut other spending
sd.dek: October data show food and beverage prices rose 15.27% in a month, while an economist says families are delaying treatment and reducing food consumption.
paragraphs: Sudan’s annual inflation rate reached 34.88% in October 2026, while the Consumer Price Index rose 6.23% from the previous month, according to the Central Bureau of Statistics. Food and beverage prices climbed 15.27% month on month and 57.23% year on year.

Economic expert Dr Wael Fahmi told Radio Dabanga that low-income families are cutting spending on healthcare, education and housing as incomes decline and people are displaced. He said they are also reducing the quantity and quality of food they consume. Healthcare accounted for only 1% of household expenditure in October, which Fahmi said reflected households’ inability to pay for medicines or hospital access and their postponement of treatment, not less need for care.

Annual inflation was 48.97% in urban areas and 26.69% in rural areas, a gap of 22.28 percentage points. Fahmi linked the difference to expanded trade in some rural markets and damage to markets, infrastructure, warehouses, electricity and water networks in cities and areas to which residents have returned.

sd.headline: UN condemns Blue Nile drone strikes that killed 17 civilians
sd.dek: The UN says the attacks came amid escalating fighting and displacement, with more than 6,700 families recently displaced at two sites in El Roseires.
paragraphs: The United Nations condemned drone strikes in Sudan’s Blue Nile state that reportedly killed 17 civilians in Ed Damazin and injured 20. Local sources said more than 40 suicide drones struck several locations on Tuesday, including the state capital and El Roseires. The Blue Nile Civil Society Initiative revised its initial toll of 15 dead and 15 injured.

The initiative blamed the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces and the Sudan People’s Liberation Movement-North, and called for an investigation. It said strikes hit homes in El Saliha and El Roseires, as well as the Okasha Club public viewing hall. UN Secretary-General spokesperson Stéphane Dujarric said the UN condemned the loss of life and called for safe, sustained humanitarian access.

A UN assessment found more than 6,700 recently displaced families at two sites in El Roseires, in need of food, clean water, healthcare and emergency shelter. Aid groups are distributing shelter materials and food and water; the UN allocated nearly $36 million this year for humanitarian programmes in Blue Nile.

sd.headline: African Union chief backs Ethiopia's proposed Sudan dialogue
sd.dek: Mahamoud Ali Youssouf says any talks must be Sudanese-led and preserve Sudan's sovereignty and unity, while the transitional government says it is ready to engage.
paragraphs: The African Union Commission Chairman, Mahamoud Ali Youssouf, said on Thursday, 26 November, that the bloc was interested in Ethiopia's proposal to host an inclusive Sudanese dialogue. In a statement from Addis Ababa, he reaffirmed the union's commitment to a peaceful, comprehensive resolution of Sudan's conflict through talks and negotiations.

Youssouf said any such process must be led and owned by Sudanese people and aim at lasting peace while preserving Sudan's sovereignty, unity and territorial integrity. Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed announced the invitation on 23 November, calling on Sudanese military, political and civilian groups to take part. Sudan's transitional government welcomed the offer, its information minister and spokesman Khalid Ahmed Danaa said.
The African Union also said it would support Burundi's President Évariste Ndayishimiye, the bloc's chair, in pursuing a lasting peaceful solution with relevant partners.

sd.headline: West Darfur launches campaign to protect women and girls from violence
sd.dek: The state began its 16 Days of Activism drive as officials and aid workers warned that war and displacement heighten risks of abuse.
paragraphs: West Darfur State launched the 16 Days of Activism Against Gender-Based Violence campaign on Wednesday, calling for action to protect women and girls and hold perpetrators accountable. The drive comes amid war-related humanitarian and security pressures in the state.

Fatima Hassan, a representative of women’s organizations, said the campaign called for concrete protection and support for survivors. She said the war had heightened risks including rape, forced marriage and child marriage. West Darfur government Secretary-General Khalil Hamid Daggarsho said displacement, refugee movements and uprooted communities had left women more vulnerable to violence, exploitation and loss of essential services.

Daggarsho said the government would work to strengthen the rule of law and develop protection and response mechanisms. World Relief’s Darfur area manager, Elijah Udo Charles, said social customs can conceal violations and called for stronger community awareness.

tg.headline: Togo police detain CBC officials as subscribers report blocked withdrawals
tg.dek: Investigators are examining the online investment platform’s network after users said they could no longer retrieve money deposited for promised daily returns.
paragraphs: Togo’s National Police have detained several people in an investigation into Curiosity Brave Compass (CBC), an online investment platform that promised daily returns. Police began looking into the company after alerts about the legality of its activities and reports of withdrawal problems and closed offices.

Police Commissioner Barry said investigators first identified an agency in Lomé’s Adido Adin neighbourhood; its managers were detained on 17 November 2026. Searches then found other agencies in Lomé and several parts of the country. Police say new members’ deposits allegedly paid earlier subscribers, and Barry compared the arrangement to a Ponzi scheme.

Investigators are trying to establish each detainee’s role, the network’s reach and whether it has members in Togo or abroad. Police have not disclosed the number of detainees or subscribers, or the total funds collected. The detainees are to be presented to the competent courts and are presumed innocent unless convicted.

tg.headline: Togo opposition groups meet in Brussels to discuss coordination
tg.dek: Organisers say the 27-29 November gathering will seek new political directions and a permanent forum for joint decisions and resolving disputes.
paragraphs: Togolese opposition parties, civil society groups and diaspora members are meeting in Brussels, Belgium, from 27 to 29 November 2026 to discuss joint action, according to 24heureinfo. The gathering, called the Brussels Assises, is organised by CODITOGO (the Togolese Coordination of Democratic Forces) and FREEDOM-TOGO MLN (a Togolese opposition movement).

The organisers’ communiqué says participants are expected to consider new directions for opposition activity and ways to bring together democratic opposition groups at home and abroad. It lists creating a permanent coordination framework and laying foundations for a broad citizen movement among the gathering’s aims.

The organisers link the meeting to a forum they held in Montreal from 14 to 17 August 2025 and to a January 2026 ruling by the Economic Community of West African States’ Court of Justice. The communiqué names no participants or detailed programme; results are expected after 29 November.

tn.headline: EU-backed programme mobilises €52.3 million for 396 Tunisian businesses
tn.dek: The €170 million Tunisia Economic Recovery programme has reached companies in 23 governorates, with financing still open to applicants.
paragraphs: Tunisia’s EU-backed Tunisia Economic Recovery programme has mobilised €52.3 million for 396 businesses across 23 governorates, Webdo reported on Friday. The programme has a total allocation of €170 million and is aimed mainly at small and medium-sized enterprises seeking funds to invest or expand.

The support includes long-term financing, grants, guarantees and technical assistance, according to Webdo. The programme also targets young entrepreneurs, women and priority governorates as it seeks to narrow regional gaps in access to finance.

Financing remains available to Tunisian businesses proposing investment, expansion or development projects. The programme is intended to support lasting job creation and strengthen the country's business base.

tn.headline: Tunisia sets weekend food discounts, chicken at 7.500 dinars
tn.dek: The 28-29 November offers cover produce and poultry in supermarkets and shops in Kef and Jendouba, with direct sales in two towns.
paragraphs: Tunisia’s Trade and Export Development Ministry scheduled food discounts for 28 and 29 November at large supermarkets and shops in Kef and Jendouba. Supermarkets will offer Thomson oranges for 1.980 dinars a kilogram, local apples for 4.500 dinars and potatoes for 2.300 dinars. Turkey cutlets will cost 16.750 dinars a kilogram.

Shops in the two governorates will cut prices on poultry products, including ready-to-cook chicken, thighs and breast, by between 1.450 and 3 dinars per kilogram; the ministry did not give final prices for each item. A direct-sales outlet opened in Ghardimaou on 26 November, and a mobile outlet is scheduled for Jerissa on 28 November, selling ready-to-cook chicken for 7.500 dinars each.
A ministry official said earlier promotions sold 225 tonnes of poultry and more than 110 tonnes of farmed fish over five weeks.

Motorists heading from central Tunis towards Ben Arous are to take Belle Vue Avenue and then 15 October Avenue, the ministry said. The ministry urged drivers to follow temporary signs and the marked diversions while the road is closed.

eh.headline: UN mission to leave Western Sahara by 31 January without holding referendum
eh.dek: MINURSO spent 35 years without organising the vote, while helping monitor the 1991 ceasefire between Morocco and the Polisario Front.
paragraphs: The United Nations Mission for the Referendum in Western Sahara (MINURSO) is due to leave the territory by 31 January 2027 without organising the self-determination referendum in its mandate, ECS Saharaui reported. The mission was created 35 years ago to let Sahrawis decide the territory's political future.

The referendum process stalled over disputes including the voter census and identification. Morocco opposed repeated efforts to update the census drawn up during Spanish rule, the report said. MINURSO also monitored the 1991 ceasefire between Morocco and the Polisario Front for decades.

Hostilities resumed in November 2020 after a Moroccan military intervention in the El Guerguerat area. Spanish journalist Ignacio Cembrero, who has followed the conflict for four decades, told RFI he fears a military escalation once the mission is gone.

ls.headline: Lesotho's acting state prosecutor warns sexual-offence cases strain her office
ls.dek: Lehlanako Mofilikoane says pressure from some parents on complainants to drop charges can also hinder cases reaching court.
paragraphs: Lesotho's Acting Director of Public Prosecutions, the country's acting chief state prosecutor, Advocate Lehlanako Mofilikoane, said her office is struggling to handle the sexual-offence cases reported each day. She made the remarks at a 16 Days of Activism event at Pioneer Mall in Maseru on Wednesday.

Mofilikoane said some parents press victims to withdraw charges against alleged perpetrators, which can obstruct cases reaching court. She urged communities to report offences and share information about the rights of women and children. Prosecutors, she said, would pursue gender-based violence cases without fear or favour and keep victims informed.
The campaign runs from 25 November to 10 December. Mofilikoane did not announce staffing or case-management changes.
